headline: Put out every forest fire, get bigger ones
dek: In 1935 the Forest Service set a deadline for every wildfire: 10 a.m. the next day.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Never another 1910
slides.text: In August 1910, fires burned more than 3 million acres in Idaho, Montana and Washington and killed at least 85 people. Ferdinand Silcox, who worked the fires, argued fire could be kept out.
slides.alt: Black and white photo of a burned hillside in 1910, covered in toppled, charred tree trunks and uprooted stumps
slides.credit: Burned site on Big Creek, St. Joe National Forest, Idaho, 1910. J.B. Halm, US Forest Service. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Out by 10 a.m.
slides.text: In 1935 Silcox, now chief, ordered every fire controlled by 10 a.m. the morning after it was reported. On western national forests, acres burned per year fell from 455,340 (1926 to 1934) to 141,975 (1935 to 1943).

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: The fuel stayed
slides.statLabel: Average US acres burned a year, 1985 to 1994 and 2016 to 2025 (NIFC). Climate and building near forests add to it.
slides.text: Small fires had kept dry pine forests open. Without them, the Forest Service says, stands of 40 to 60 trees an acre grew to hundreds, and fuel piled up for bigger, hotter fires.
slides.alt: Satellite view of a huge wildfire in forested mountains, with long plumes of smoke streaming north over green and brown land
slides.credit: The Dixie Fire, California, August 4, 2021, seen by Landsat 7. NASA Earth Observatory. Public domain.

slides.label: Second act
slides.title: The idea comes back
slides.text: In May 2025 the Forest Service chief wrote that it is critical to suppress fires as swiftly as possible, with risk informed efforts to put out small fires before they grow. In July 2026 he told Congress every fire has a full suppression strategy.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Partly
slides.text: In 1935 Elers Koch, who fought the 1910 fires, argued that remote backcountry should be left to burn. In 1943 Harold Weaver warned that keeping all fire out was harming pine forests. How much fuel would pile up took decades to show.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Putting fire back
slides.text: Parks began letting some fires burn in 1968, the Forest Service in 1972, and it dropped the policy in 1978. In 2022 it set out to thin or burn up to 20 million more acres in 10 years.
slides.alt: Low flames creep through pine needles on the floor of an open ponderosa pine forest during a planned burn, with smoke among the trunks
slides.credit: Prescribed burn in ponderosa pine, Grand Canyon National Park, December 11, 2024. National Park Service. Public domain.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Acres burned per year on western national forests: 455,340 in 1926 to 1934, 141,975 in 1935 to 1943 (Loveridge, Journal of Forestry, 1944)
No long-running blowup fire on western national forests from 1935 to 1944, the agency reported (same source)
By the 1950s and 1960s, area burned each year was a fraction of its historical extent (US Forest Service, 2022)
costs: Dry pine stands that once had 40 to 60 trees an acre now have hundreds in many places (US Forest Service, 2022)
Average US acres burned a year: 3.0 million in 1985 to 1994, 7.1 million in 2016 to 2025, from fewer fires (NIFC)
Fire took 52% of the Forest Service budget in 2015, up from 16% in 1995 (USDA)
slides.text: It stopped the fires of its day. It also left the fuel those fires would have burned. Climate and building near forests added to the bill. You decide if it was worth it.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: Credit where due
slides.text: Silcox took on a real problem: long, costly fire seasons and the memory of 1910. The policy was recommended without a dissent by 20 regional foresters and research directors, and it did what it was built to do. It outlived him by 39 years.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: Every fire out, every log left
slides.text: Each small fire put out left its fuel standing. Most fires were caught small, so the few that got away burned on the hottest, windiest days, through decades of stored fuel. One review says suppression left only the most extreme fire behavior.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your code freeze does it too
slides.text: Every risky deploy gets held, so nothing small breaks. The changes queue up behind the freeze. Then the quarter ends, and they all ship at once in one release nobody can debug. The small failures were how the risk used to get out.

items.risk: Fuel builds up where small fires used to clear it
items.softened: Keep some low, cool fire in dry pine forests, as light burning advocates and Koch argued at the time
items.question: What small failures are we preventing, and what were they releasing?

items.risk: The fires that escape are the worst ones
items.softened: Plan for the fire that gets away, not only for catching fires small
items.question: What happens on the day the protection fails?

items.softened: Weigh spending against what is at risk, the rule the 1935 policy set aside
items.question: What does this cost in twenty years, and who pays then?

slides.label: What if?
slides.title: What if Koch had won in 1935?
slides.text: Speculation: had the Forest Service let remote backcountry fires burn from 1935, as Koch proposed, not from 1972, parts of the northern Rockies might have kept a patchwork of recent burns. Later studies there found recently burned ground burns less severely.

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: Small failures can be doing a job nobody wrote down.
A fix judged by what it stops this year can hide what it stores up.
The better a system is at stopping small failures, the more the one that gets through has to work with.
